title: Ep 298: SpotDraft's Shashank Bijapur: From Late-Night Due Diligence to Legal Tech Innovation
author: Shashank Bijapur

dom.t: Adoption leadership: Trust must follow customer outcomes

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Bijapur does not address whether automation weakens apprenticeship or partner succession. He instead shifts the focus to AI-agent supervision as a prospective role and billing incentives as the principal constraint on law-firm adoption, offering an adjacent operating-model and commercial framing rather than support for the cluster’s expertise-pipeline proposition.
qs: I would not be surprised to see a law firm or a legal department have a manager that manages AI agents.
I keep hearing about law firms wanting to do it because they want to be more accurate and efficient, but something's got to change in the way they bill in order for this to work.

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: Bijapur anticipates AI-agent oversight and argues that billing incentives will shape law-firm adoption, but he does not address whether automation undermines associate apprenticeship, creates a verification-expertise paradox, or requires reconstructed training. His position on the cluster’s principal proposition therefore cannot be determined.
qs: I would not be surprised to see a law firm or a legal department have a manager that manages AI agents.
I keep hearing about law firms wanting to do it because they want to be more accurate and efficient, but something's got to change in the way they bill in order for this to work.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s distinction between AI demand and demonstrated outcomes, noting poorly defined objectives and adoption barriers such as billing incentives. However, it addresses commercial legal organisations rather than access to justice and provides no evidence or explicit view on whether AI uptake can close justice gaps.
qs: But very few companies really know to what outcome.
I keep hearing about law firms wanting to do it because they want to be more accurate and efficient, but something's got to change in the way they bill in order for this to work.

st.t: Task substitution: Complementarity can still reshape staffing
st.an: The source supports broad task-level substitution within an assistant model, but it provides only product claims and does not address resulting staffing, demand, employment or business-model changes. The near-autonomy forecast is introduced by the interviewer without Bijapur’s substantive response, so it cannot establish the source’s position on the cluster’s central proposition.
qs: So you can do pretty much everything that you would want your legal team to do, whether it's raising tickets, whether it is answering uh questions on a contract, or just doing research, all of that end-to-end uh using that platform.
Yes, it is a legal assistant because it's still a legal assistant and at some point when  it gets better and smarter, hopefully uh it can take on a different name.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source develops the cluster’s operating-model proposition in the specific context of contracting: existing CLM architecture becomes the foundation for conversational, AI-assisted workflows and connected-data insights, rather than being displaced by a standalone model. Its forecast that AI will complete about 80% of an NDA workflow also implies bounded assistance rather than complete autonomy, although it does not address verification, user expertise or governance.
qs: And most of the things that are CLM today will form the architecture of how some of the more basic questions are answered and workflows work through.

We expect them to go into a dialogue box and say, hey, can you create a contract, uh create an NDA with John Doe, similar to the one that we created with Jane, David, for yesterday, and for it to get you to 80 % of the way and get the rest of the questions answered.

st.t: Adoption leadership: Trust must follow customer outcomes
st.an: Bijapur supports the cluster’s emphasis on experimentation, customer–provider collaboration and user-led improvement. His account of LLM-assisted learning is personal experience, while his product claims and invitations are promotional rather than demonstrated outcome evidence.
qs: But more than that, it is now more than ever that we need the support and sort of the evangelism of people who are willing to try new products and talk about how this makes a change.
So the offices of Spodraft are always open to have discussions on how we can do better or what we should build next.

st.t: Agentic delegation: Multistep work moves verification bottlenecks
st.an: Bijapur supports the cluster’s core view that legal AI is moving toward connected, end-to-end workflows and will require humans to manage delegated agents. His claims about grounding and anticipated accuracy are promotional or predictive rather than measured evidence, consistent with the cluster’s caution that current deployment accounts do not establish broad reliability or autonomous readiness.
qs: So you can do pretty much everything that you would want your legal team to do, whether it's raising tickets, whether it is answering uh questions on a contract, or just doing research, all of that end-to-end uh using that platform.
I would not be surprised to see a law firm or a legal department have a manager that manages AI agents.

st.t: Agentic workflows: Tacit expertise resists easy transfer
st.an: SpotDraft’s account supports the cluster’s core proposition that practical legal AI depends on more than prompting: Bijapur attributes Sidebar’s capabilities to accumulated data, learning and proprietary development, while presenting connected workflow assistance rather than established full autonomy. Its broad capability and accuracy claims remain company-reported and unvalidated, consistent with the cluster’s evidentiary caution.
qs: And we've been able to do this not as a wrapper on a LLM with a few smart prompts at the  back end.
We're doing this uh with data points that we have learned, we have developed, and with a lot of uh proprietary uh IP that's gone into building this.

st.t: Conditional optimism: User problems outrank AI branding
st.an: Bijapur aligns with the cluster’s conditional, user-led optimism: he describes the LLM as an assistant for learning and internal analysis, not autonomous decision-making, and calls for users to experiment and provide product feedback. His account is experiential and promotional rather than measured proof of performance or transformation.
qs: So uh my sidekick is an LLM to just help me understand and learn more.
So the offices of Spodraft are always open to have discussions on how we can do better or what we should build next.

st.t: Contract infrastructure: AI challenges siloed CLM systems
st.an: Bijapur supports the synthesis’s core view that AI will change contract-system architecture without eliminating contract-management functions. He takes the continuity side of the unresolved dispute, forecasting that CLM capabilities will remain the foundation for conversational contracting and AI-driven workflows; this is a prospective claim, not comparative performance evidence.
qs: And most of the things that are CLM today will form the architecture of how some of the more basic questions are answered and workflows work through.

And I feel like uh while it's an incorrect comparison to say CLM is the DVD business equivalent, but it is going to be very much uh the backbone and the foundation of how this new streaming business or the AI-driven business will work.

st.t: Contract intelligence: Business coordination exceeds document storage
st.an: Bijapur supports the cluster’s broader view that contract technology should enable workflows and actionable intelligence rather than function only as document storage. He specifically argues that CLM capabilities will remain the foundation for AI-driven questions and workflows, with conversational interfaces and connected data producing new insights; these are forecasts, not measured outcomes.
qs: And most of the things that are CLM today will form the architecture of how some of the more basic questions are answered and workflows work through.
And we see this as a way in which it's able to connect different pieces of data and get you insights.

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source supports the synthesis by arguing that in-house efficiency incentives may accelerate adoption, while law-firm billing structures impede substantive deployment. It also reinforces the synthesis’s caution that strong buyer demand has not yet translated into clearly defined outcomes or measured effectiveness; its agent-manager claim remains predictive.
qs: I keep hearing about law firms wanting to do it because they want to be more accurate and efficient, but something's got to change in the way they bill in order for this to work.
But very few companies really know to what outcome.

st.t: In-house adoption: Stronger buyers may insource selectively
st.an: The source supports the synthesis by contrasting in-house teams’ stronger efficiency incentives with law firms’ billing constraints and by reporting substantial buyer demand for AI. It also reinforces the synthesis’s caution that procurement interest does not itself establish effective adoption or outcomes, because companies often cannot define the results sought. It does not directly demonstrate insourcing or reduced outside-counsel spending.
qs: In-house teams, I feel, will see a lot more will be more welcoming to something like this because they need to see that efficiency.
But very few companies really know to what outcome.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Bijapur’s account supports the cluster’s view that generative AI extends specialist legal workflow software rather than replacing it overnight. SpotDraft combines contract-specific functions with accumulated data, analytics and earlier language-model work, while its claims remain founder-reported rather than comparative performance evidence. The source does not materially address human verification or the durability of specialist layers against improving general models.
qs: We're a contract management and automation platform that helps businesses create, manage, analyze, and collaborate on contracts.
And then we were sitting on data, we were sitting on analytics, we were sitting on learnings, we were working off BERT, which was the state of the art before LLMs came in.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: Bijapur supports the cluster’s central view that legal AI value depends on moving beyond generic capability into substantive legal context, practical use and adoption support. SpotDraft’s experience also reinforces the cluster’s caution that vendor feedback and commercial expectations are weaker evidence than measured legal outcomes; the source does not materially address verification or lawyer control.
qs: Now with GenAI coming in, you're going from what was predominantly operational problem, you're cutting three layers deep and you're going inside the law and figuring out whether that works for you or not.
They don't know how it is important and how to use it.

st.t: Service model: AI challenges production more than lawyers
st.an: Bijapur supports the synthesis’s hybrid, buyer-led account: he expects in-house teams to embrace AI for efficiency, sees law-firm billing as a barrier to substantive adoption, and still frames the product as an assistant rather than autonomous legal delivery. His broader capability and accuracy assertions are vendor claims without independent validation.
qs: In-house teams, I feel, will see a lot more will be more welcoming to something like this because they need to see that efficiency.
I keep hearing about law firms wanting to do it because they want to be more accurate and efficient, but something's got to change in the way they bill in order for this to work.

st.t: Vendor strategy: Faster building cannot eliminate integration
st.an: SpotDraft’s account supports the synthesis’s adoption-side proposition: customer receptiveness varies, requiring deliberate targeting and practical product fit, while generative AI advances an existing strategic ambition rather than removing implementation constraints. It does not provide evidence about faster development, migration, or integration economics.
qs: But we realized very quickly that lawyers are not very receptive to change.
Yeah, mean, so for us, this is a natural evolution of where we wanted to be but failed.

kp.k: Early redlining failure drove a data-focused CLM pivot
kp.d: Bijapur says SpotDraft was incorporated in 2017, began coding in 2018, and initially targeted contract redlining and negotiation. He describes its early accuracy as 60%, attributing failure to insufficient data. Building a contracting editor, workflows and a repository led the company to adopt the CLM label in 2020, originally to improve its redlining capability. This is a founder's retrospective account, not an independently evaluated accuracy result.
qs: 2017 was when the company was incorporated. 18 was first line of code between Madhav and me.
But then we realized in a couple of years that we were as good as a coin toss, which is 60 % accurate, and that wasn't going anywhere.
We didn't have enough data.
that's in 2020 was when we used the word CLM for the first time, just so that we could get better understanding of data to build a better redlining platform.

kp.k: Growth-stage legal teams enabled early product development
kp.d: Bijapur reports that early customers helped co-build a software product rather than commission a services business. He identifies lawyers at rapidly scaling companies as more willing to accept change and bugs, making them suitable initial adopters of an experimental platform. SpotDraft now describes its focus as contract creation, management, analysis and collaboration for high-growth businesses, including accelerating quote-to-cash processes.
qs: also understood that this wasn't a services company. We were building a product
those tend to be in uh growth stage companies, companies that were scaling very quickly, they were okay with breaking things and bugs were fine.
We're a contract management and automation platform that helps businesses create, manage, analyze, and collaborate on contracts.

kp.k: Implementation and adoption underpin vendor differentiation
kp.d: Bijapur attributes CLM implementation failures primarily to poor adoption or implementation, without supplying a failure rate or study. He positions SpotDraft's vendor-funded implementation and customer support as competitive differentiators, arguing that lawyers need assistance choosing and promoting technology within legal teams and their wider organisations.
qs: First was it was poorly adopted or it was poorly implemented and we offset both of them.
We do implementation on our own dime and we do it in record time.
Lawyers were not meant to buy technology that's not their strongest suite. So we make it easier for them

kp.k: Generative AI extends CLM into substantive legal analysis
kp.d: Bijapur distinguishes traditional CLM's operational benefits—structured intake, visibility and streamlined contracting—from generative AI's ability to examine the legal substance of contracts. He presents this as a qualitatively different value proposition and an opportunity for vendors to deepen their role within customer organisations, rather than reporting measured improvements in legal quality.
qs: Nobody became a better lawyer using a CLM. What happened is that process of contracting became way more streamlined.

Now with GenAI coming in, you're going from what was predominantly operational problem, you're cutting three layers deep and you're going inside the law and figuring out whether that works for you or not.

kp.k: Sidebar expands assistance beyond contract lifecycle management
kp.d: Bijapur describes Sidebar as a legal assistant for contract questions, research and ticket creation that can operate with or without a CLM. He says it detects changes in contracts and the outside world and uses proprietary learning and data rather than merely prompts around a model. General-public launch is described as next month. Positive design-partner feedback and predictions of exceptional accuracy are vendor-reported claims, not independent findings; his initial assertion of no hallucinations is immediately qualified.
qs: We recently launched Sidebar and it's launching for the general public next month.
It is grounded, so it never hallucinates, or rather, there is very little chance that it hallucinates.
it works very well with either a CLM or without a CLM.
whether it's raising tickets, whether it is answering uh questions on a contract, or just doing research, all of that end-to-end uh using that platform.

kp.k: AI-agent management may emerge first in-house
kp.d: Responding to the host's question about increasingly autonomous assistants, Bijapur predicts that firms or legal departments could employ managers of AI agents. He expects in-house teams to be more receptive because they need efficiency. His prediction for law firms is conditional: billing practices must change for AI to move beyond an R&D allocation into substantive development. He provides neither a timetable nor a specific replacement billing model.
qs: I would not be surprised to see a law firm or a legal department have a manager that manages AI agents.
In-house teams, I feel, will see a lot more will be more welcoming to something like this because they need to see that efficiency.
something's got to change in the way they bill in order for this to work. Otherwise, all of this is going to get into the R &D budget and not really into true product development on that segment.

kp.k: AI demand exceeds clarity about intended outcomes
kp.d: From customer conversations and RFPs, Bijapur reports intense interest in AI but limited ability to specify desired outcomes or effective uses. He contrasts this with the pre-LLM period, when vendors had to explain AI's basic capabilities and counter unrealistic expectations. These are commercial observations; although the host references SpotDraft's April survey, the transcript provides no sample size, methodology or quantified adoption findings.
qs: We don't have a single conversation where the word AI is not brought up as a requirement.
we are beginning to see RFPs where some uh loosely sort of defined version of AI needs to be there. But very few companies really know to what outcome.
People know that AI is important. They don't know how it is important and how to use it.

kp.k: Training rights and sourced accuracy anchor trust claims
kp.d: Asked about security and ethics concerns, Bijapur emphasises rights to training data, accuracy, trusted legal sources and declining to answer rather than offering unsupported responses. He says customers may abandon tools after three unsuccessful attempts, making accuracy central to adoption. He also describes removing the need for explicit prompting. The answer supplies product assurances rather than measured error rates or detailed security controls.
qs: making sure that the data that we trained on was ethically correct and we had the rights to train on them.
We've seen this behavior with customers where they're going to try things for three times, and if it doesn't work the way they want it to work, they probably will not use it.
either we don't answer the question or we answer the question as then close to the law as possible with the right sources.
The word prompting uh does not come up.

kp.k: Adoption advice emphasises junior-level assistance and legal-team control
kp.d: Bijapur recommends treating AI like a first-day law graduate rather than an experienced lawyer, expecting it to get 70–80% of the way and correcting mistakes. These percentages express recommended expectations, not benchmark results. He says SpotDraft prioritises in-house lawyers as initial adopters before wider internal promotion. Although a Slack bot answers end-user questions, he explicitly distances the current approach from sales representatives treating it as an actual lawyer.
qs: think of this as you fresh out of law school, first day at your job.
Look at it as something that gets you 70%, 80 % of the way. tell it when it's wrong so that it's able to improve.
we are currently focused on ensuring that in-house legal teams are the first adopters before they evangelize internally within the company.
But we've not yet built it with the sales rep coming and asking the question and believing this is an actual lawyer answering.

kp.k: Conversational interfaces could replace manual CLM interactions
kp.d: Bijapur forecasts that within two years users will request contracts through dialogue rather than clicking through creation workflows and questionnaires. His example is generating an NDA by reference to an earlier transaction, getting 80% of the way before resolving remaining questions. He expects CLM repositories and workflows to remain the underlying infrastructure, with AI connecting data to produce new insights. He uses Netflix's DVD-to-streaming transition as a qualified analogy, not empirical evidence.
qs: We don't expect the customer two years down the line to go in there and say, click new. create new contract, answer a few questions.

We expect them to go into a dialogue box and say, hey, can you create a contract, uh create an NDA with John Doe, similar to the one that we created with Jane, David, for yesterday, and for it to get you to 80 % of the way and get the rest of the questions answered.
it is going to be very much uh the backbone and the foundation of how this new streaming business or the AI-driven business will work.

kp.k: Integrated workflow data supports claimed advantage over point solutions
kp.d: Challenging a point-solution argument reported by the host, Bijapur contends that legal AI needs collaboration histories and repositories to understand how contracts evolve. He highlights version sequences and interactions between sales and legal as important training material, predicting Sidebar will outperform standalone AI tools. This is a vendor's competitive thesis, with no comparative evaluation supplied.
qs: How do you build a system of intelligence without the system of collaboration and that repository that has seen that data flow through?
never having trained on version one through version 23, knowing that Sam from sales comes in and puts a comment, and then Bob from Legal goes and makes that change.
I feel like something... like SpotDraft with its sidebar platform will be far superior than a standalone AI-only platform.

kp.k: Funding signals perceived maturation of legal technology
kp.d: The host reports a $54 million Series B raised in February and a $26 million Series A in 2023. Bijapur interprets growing investor interest specifically in legal technology as a sign of the sector's coming of age, attributing it to customer support, employees and industry advocacy. He identifies research and development and team-building as major uses of the funding; the investment figures are reported financing events, not evidence of achieved product performance.
qs: You raised $54 million in a series B round just in February. You had previously raised $26 million in a Series A round in 2023.
Legal tech went from being, you know, a small footnote somewhere to having its own line item.
a large chunk of it obviously is towards uh R &B. We're also investing heavily in building a world-class team.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Bijapur says generative AI extends contract technology beyond workflow organisation into substantive legal analysis.
pts.d: He contrasts traditional CLM's operational benefits—structured intake, visibility and streamlined contracting—with generative AI's ability to examine the law and whether contractual provisions work for a business. He anticipates substantial impact from language models in legal work, but not immediate transformation.

pts.k: Bijapur presents Sidebar as a source-grounded legal assistant spanning contract questions, research and internal requests, with unusually high anticipated accuracy.
pts.d: He claims Sidebar can track changes in contracts and the outside world, operate with or without a CLM, and perform multiple legal-team tasks. He immediately qualifies an initial claim that it never hallucinates to say there is very little chance of hallucination. Its projected standing among the most accurate legal AI products is his vendor prediction, rather than a reported comparative test result.

pts.k: Bijapur predicts AI-agent management roles and faster acceptance in corporate legal departments than in law firms.
pts.d: He expects a law firm or legal department could have a manager supervising AI agents. He regards in-house efficiency incentives as favourable to adoption, while making substantive law-firm deployment conditional on changes to billing. He does not forecast lawyer headcount reductions or specify when these roles will emerge.

pts.k: Bijapur says AI demand is widespread among prospective customers, but clarity about outcomes and implementation remains limited.
pts.d: He describes AI as a routine requirement in customer conversations and an emerging, often loosely defined requirement in RFPs. Relative to the pre-LLM period, he reports greater awareness of both AI's capabilities and limitations, reducing basic market-education work without eliminating the need to explain practical uses.

pts.k: Bijapur recommends treating current legal AI as a junior assistant that advances work partway, receives corrections and improves over time.
pts.d: His current deployment framing is augmentation, not autonomous substitution for an experienced lawyer. He tells users to expect roughly 70–80% progress and provide corrective feedback, and claims SpotDraft's system learns over time from that feedback. These percentages are an expectation-setting description, not a disclosed benchmark. He prioritises legal-team adoption before wider business use and explicitly distinguishes the product from an actual lawyer answering a sales representative.

pts.k: Bijapur predicts conversational contract creation will replace click-based interactions while CLM remains the underlying infrastructure.
pts.d: He expects users to request contracts through dialogue, referring to previous agreements rather than completing conventional interface steps. The system would get a draft approximately 80% complete and obtain the remaining information. He also predicts connections across data will yield previously unavailable insights; this is a forecast rather than an observed performance result.

pts.k: Bijapur argues that collaboration histories and contract repositories give integrated CLM-based AI an advantage over standalone AI tools.
pts.d: He links useful redlining intelligence to training on actual revisions, comments and negotiation sequences. He predicts Sidebar will outperform standalone AI-only platforms because of these data and workflow foundations, while acknowledging that some point solutions will do well. This is his competitive argument as SpotDraft's CEO.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered is primarily Bijapur's product-development experience, customer observations and design-partner feedback.
pts.d: For the importance of data, he recounts the early redlining product's approximately 60% accuracy and attributes its failure to insufficient data; no test methodology or sample is given. For Sidebar's quality, he cites design-partner reactions, accumulated data, proprietary development, source grounding and internal use. For adoption claims, he relies on sales conversations, RFPs and observed customer behaviour. A SpotDraft survey is mentioned during the interview, but no survey findings with sample sizes, methods or numerical results are supplied in his answers. The transcript supplies no independent comparative benchmark supporting the accuracy or superiority predictions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The interview distinguishes current assisted use from a two-year interface forecast and undated agent-management and market-superiority predictions.
pts.d: At the 2025 interview, Sidebar is described as recently launched, with general-public availability expected the following month. The conversational-interface forecast is explicitly two years ahead, within a discussion prompted by a five-year outlook. Agent-management roles, broader legal impact and superiority over standalone AI have no fixed dates. Present usefulness is qualified by partial completion, feedback, trusted sources and abstention when the system cannot answer. Bijapur also identifies accuracy and ease of use as conditions for continued adoption, and billing reform as a condition for substantive law-firm uptake.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are in-house legal teams at high-growth businesses, their internal business users, law firms and competing legal-technology vendors.
pts.d: Corporate legal teams are the immediate users of assisted drafting, research and contract analysis, with potential efficiency gains and future responsibilities supervising agents. High-growth businesses are SpotDraft's stated customer focus, with faster quote-to-cash processes as a business objective. Sales teams and other internal users are prospective downstream beneficiaries, but rollout is legal-team-first. Law firms face the billing-incentive constraint identified by Bijapur. Integrated CLM vendors and standalone AI vendors face the competitive shift he predicts. SpotDraft is discussed as a software provider, not an alternative legal service provider; the interview offers no concrete prediction about access to justice or employment displacement.
